newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey says Iraqi oil to flow, hopes trade revival.
newsitem.headline: Turkey says Iraqi oil to flow, hopes trade revival.

text.p: Turkey said on Thursday that by mid-December Iraqi oil should start flowing to the market again under a long-awaited U.N. plan and Turkish businesses expect a revival in trade with the country's southeastern neighbour.

"Iraqi oil will start flowing by December 15 at the latest through the Kirkuk-Yumurtalik pipeline," State Minister Lutfi Esengun told reporters after a cabinet meeting, referring to the U.N. plan that allows Baghdad to sell oil worth $2 billion over six months to buy food and medicine.
"All remaining obstacles will be removed in the next 15 days and the pipeline will become operational and begin carrying oil," he said, without giving details.
The head of the Iraqi delegation to the OPEC meeting said in Vienna that renewed oil exports could move by mid-December.

The oil-for-food deal moved closer to being activated when Iraq earlier this month unconditionally accepted terms of the May 20 U.N. accord. Jordan, which is on Iraq's Western border, is also hoping for a boost in trade once the deal takes effect.
Turkey earlier said the twin pipeline from Iraq's Kirkuk oilfields to Turkey's southern Ceyhan terminal were technically ready to handle the Iraqi oil sales under the U.N. plan.
The plan envisages that Iraq sell most of the oil through this pipeline and the rest via its southern Mina Al-Bakr oil terminal.

Turkish officials were not immediately available for comment on the status of the oil trapped inside the pipeline and whether the 12 tanks at the Ceyhan terminal were completely full of oil -- something that will facilitate quicker movement of the oil out of the pipeline when it starts flowing again.
But oil officials earlier said there were 12 million barrels of oil inside the twin pipelines, of which about 3.8 million barrels belong to Turkey.
They said the thinner, 40-inch-diameter, but longer pipeline would be used for Iraqi sales. This 986-km (616-mile) line can carry up to 46.5 million tonnes a year.

Iraq pumped an average 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) of oil, or nearly two-thirds of its total oil exports, through the pipeline before the U.N. embargo imposed after its invasion of Kuwait in 1990.
Oil analysts said Iraq's exports could be 700,000 to 800,000 bpd under the current prices.

The Dutch firm Saybolt, picked by the United Nations to monitor oil exports and make sure oil metering equipment works properly, said it was still awaiting U.N. instructions to send their full team of 14 experts to Iraq.
A team of Lloyd's Shipping has already begun inspections at Iraq's trade outlets.

Iraq will use $1.3 billion of the total oil sales for its food and medicine purchases. Turkish companies have already been selling Iraq basic foodstuffs, mostly wheat flour, pulses and sugar, under U.N. auspices since the sanctions took effect.
Turkish traders and businessmen were chasing the lion's share in the limited trade with Iraq, trying to get the best out of their geographical proximity to Iraq.
Abdulkadir Cikmaz, head of Turkey's Southeast Grain Exporters Union, said Turkish exporters might sell goods worth a total of $700 million to Iraq under the U.N. plan.
"We can sell $150 million worth food and medicine for northern Iraqis only. And also goods worth $400-$500 million can be sold to Iraq itself," he told Reuters.
Turkey will also receive about $50 million from transit fees on the use of the pipeline, according to the U.N. plan.

Officials said an government circular sent to the customs at Turkey's Habur crossing with Iraq would allow Turkish trucks, which carry food items to northern Iraq, to bring back up to four tonnes of cheap Iraqi diesel instead of the present two tonnes to finance their trips.
"This will also reduce a possible shortage of diesel due to the recent closure of Atas refinery," an official said.
The refinery, operated by Mobil and Royal Dutch/Shell and located at southern port of Mersin, was closed last month due to financial crisis.
Turkey's state oil refinery Tupras had asked to buy 2.1 million tonnes from Iraq's oil sales.
